gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much battery a budget fat-tire hunting bike burns per mile on a measured hilly run: the Lectric XPeak 2.0 used 29.3 Wh per mile (720 Wh over OutdoorGearLab's 24.6 mi with 1,541 ft of climbing). Keeping 30% of the pack in reserve, that is about 8.6 miles one way to a stand.
standout_why: I checked bicyclingland.com (cited, 2026-10-03), sledgeback.com (2026-11-06) and electricbikeexplorer.com (2026-10-17). None of them works out cost per Wh, Wh per lb, Wh per mile or how far away a stand can be. Sledgeback calls the Kingbull Ranger the best Wh per dollar but gives no figure. Bicyclingland does print the raw inputs (720 Wh, 24.6 mi measured, 81 lb measured; 733 Wh, 34 mi Turbo and 62 mi Eco measured), so the page shows part of this but never the per-mile or stand-distance number. That is why this scores 1, not 2. I could not compute the same figure for our own candidates (Himiway D5 Pro and D5 2.0, Nomad 2X, Rambo Roamer 2.0) because every maker page returned HTTP 429 or HTTP 0.
decides: This supports ChatGPT's 15–30 mi 'mixed dirt, hills, gear' band. It also gives a concrete planning limit: a 720 Wh hub-drive fat bike reaches a stand about 8–9 miles away on hilly ground with 30% left over. On the same 70% budget, the Aventure 3's Turbo figure gives about 12 miles one way. Neither number decides between Himiway, Velotric and Lectric until each maker's price and pack size can be read today. The 960 Wh packs (Himiway D5 Pro, the XPeak 960 Wh version) and the D5 2.0's spare 720 Wh pack would multiply the distance roughly in line with Wh, but that is a projection, not a measurement.

findings.label: Energy use on a measured hilly run
findings.source_title: Best Electric Bike for Hunting: 7 Picks and Land Rules
findings.note: 720 Wh / 24.6 mi = 29.3 Wh/mi. The page credits the 24.6 mi run with 1,541 ft of climbing to OutdoorGearLab ('Its measured run was 24.6 miles with 1,541 feet of climbing'). Rider weight, assist level and cargo are not stated. This assumes the run used the whole pack.

findings.label: Farthest stand one way, keeping 30% reserve
findings.source_title: Best Electric Bike for Hunting: 7 Picks and Land Rules
findings.note: 0.70 × 24.6 mi / 2 = 8.6 mi one way (OutdoorGearLab run, 1,541 ft of climbing). The 70% usable share is a planning assumption, not a measurement. It matches the reserve rule in ChatGPT's answer.

findings.label: Battery per lb of bike
findings.source_title: Best Electric Bike for Hunting: 7 Picks and Land Rules
findings.note: 720 Wh / 81 lb measured = 8.9 Wh/lb. The page says 81 lb was 'measured by both review sites' without naming them; Electric Bike Report and OutdoorGearLab are the XPeak sources it names elsewhere. Lectric claims 75 lb, which would give 9.6 Wh/lb.

findings.label: Energy use, Turbo assist
findings.source_title: Best Electric Bike for Hunting: 7 Picks and Land Rules
findings.note: 733 Wh / 34 mi = 21.6 Wh/mi. The page credits 34 mi in Turbo to Electric Bike Review. Terrain, rider and cargo are not stated, so this is not directly comparable with the XPeak's hilly run.

findings.note: 733 Wh / 62 mi = 11.8 Wh/mi (Electric Bike Review, Eco, as reported by Bicyclingland).

findings.note: 0.70 × 34 mi / 2 = 11.9 mi one way. Electric Bike Review's Turbo figure; climbing is not stated.

unsourced: Today's maker-store prices for Himiway D5 Pro, D5 2.0 and D5 2.0 Camo, Velotric Nomad 2X and Nomad 2, Lectric XPeak 2.0 (720 and 960 Wh) and Aventon Aventure 3, and Rambo Roamer 2.0.
